lines.text: Some of the oldest cities on Earth, the seat of caliphs, a prize for crusaders and empires, and a nation torn by war. This is the story of Syria.
In the north, people settled at Aleppo some seven thousand years ago, and it has been lived in ever since, beneath its great citadel.
Nearby, the city of Ebla flourished and kept a great archive of clay tablets, one of the richest records of the ancient world.
To the south, Damascus grew into one of the oldest cities still lived in anywhere, and in time the country's capital.
After Alexander the Great, his general Seleucus founded an empire that spread Greek cities and culture across Syria and western Asia.
Under Rome, Queen Zenobia of Palmyra ruled for her young son and seized Egypt and much of the Roman east, until the emperor Aurelian defeated her.
With the spread of Islam, Damascus became the capital of the Umayyad caliphs, whose empire reached from Spain to the borders of India.
In Damascus they built the Great Mosque, the Umayyad Mosque, one of the grandest in the Islamic world.
Centuries later, crusaders held the coast. Saladin, born a Kurd, united Egypt and Syria against them and took back Jerusalem.
The Knights Hospitaller held Krak des Chevaliers, among the strongest castles of its time, until the Mamluks captured it in 1271.
After four centuries of Ottoman rule, the empire collapsed in the First World War, and in 1920 a Syrian state was declared, only to fall under France.
In Damascus, Nizar Qabbani was born. He would become one of the best-loved Arab poets, of love and of politics.
France ruled Syria and Lebanon under a mandate for more than twenty years.
Hafez al-Assad was born, an air force officer who would seize power and rule Syria for three decades.
In April 1946 the last French troops left. Syria celebrates the day as its national holiday.
In 1958 Syria joined Egypt in the United Arab Republic, but the union broke apart after just three years.
Bashar al-Assad was born, a son of Hafez who would inherit his rule in 2000.
In 1982 the regime crushed an uprising in the city of Hama, killing thousands.
That same year Ahmed al-Sharaa was born, a future rebel leader and president.
Meanwhile a jihadist group took shape that would later call itself Islamic State, and seize much of Syria and Iraq.
In 2011 protests against Bashar al-Assad were met with force, and grew into a civil war that killed hundreds of thousands and drove millions from home.
Aleppo became a battlefield for four years, its ancient old town ruined, until the regime took it in 2016.
In 2013 sarin gas was used near Damascus, in the Ghouta, killing hundreds of people.
In 2015 a photograph of a drowned three-year-old Syrian boy on a Turkish beach moved the world to face the refugee crisis.
Then, in December 2024, rebels swept into Damascus. Bashar al-Assad fled, and more than fifty years of family rule came to an end.
After so much loss, Syria's ancient story turns once more to a new and uncertain chapter.
